tagline.text: A protected landscape in western Pangasinan with a forest hot spring and birdsong

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱100~400 (per person for a half day, meals only; entrance, cottage and transport not included)

children.text: Manleluag Spring is a hot spring inside a protected landscape in Mangatarem, western Pangasinan. Hot spring pools, forest paths and a view deck in a small woodland make it a quiet half-day stop.
The Manleluag Spring Protected Landscape lies in Barangay Malabobo, Mangatarem, Pangasinan. It is about
180km

north of Manila, and the nearest city is San Carlos. Pangasinan has only two protected areas: Hundred Islands in Alaminos and this one. It suits travelers who want to add an inland hot spring and some forest to a Pangasinan trip that is otherwise centered on beaches.
Its designation history is long and has changed several times. It began in 1934 as a spring forest reserve of about
, and in 1939 an adjoining
of public forest was added. On September 3, 1940, President Quezon redesignated it a national park of about

under Proclamation No. 612, and on March 10, 2004, President Arroyo converted it into a protected landscape (IUCN Category V) under Proclamation No. 576. It is now managed by the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR).
The whole protected landscape covers about
, of which about

is the recreation zone. The rest is divided into wildlife habitat, sustainable use and restoration zones, so the forest remains relatively intact. The springs are two ophiolitic hot springs rising at the foot of Mount Malabobo, an extinct volcano about
high, and local information describes the water as strongly alkaline, with a pH of 11 to 13. By zone, wildlife habitat is about
, sustainable use about
, multiple use about
and restoration about

. In other words, the part visitors actually use is a very small share, and most of the area is conserved as forest and habitat. The forest is part of the Mangatarem forest, which stretches across Pangasinan, Zambales and Tarlac in the Zambales Mountains.

For visitors this is not a showy resort but a small park in the woods. Three hot spring pools, a children's pool, a pavilion, paved concrete walkways and a view deck are the essentials. It is quiet and simple, so plan on bringing your own food and drinks.
Water from a small cemented reservoir flows into three pools of different temperatures. The smallest pool, closest to the spring, is the hottest, and the largest is about
deep and described as suitable for swimming and diving. No exact water temperature was confirmed, so ease in slowly.
A children's pool beside the largest pool makes this workable for families. A small pavilion is said to be usable for parties, meetings and gatherings.

Concrete-paved paths run through the small woodland, easy to walk even in sandals. Around the protected landscape there are also separate patrol trails and fire lines for forest fire protection, which are distinct from the visitor paths.
Local tourism information mentions a view deck tower overlooking the green landscape of Mangatarem. Check its status when you visit.

More than 90 bird species are reported here, including the Philippine frogmouth, rufous hornbill and Philippine hanging parrot. One visitor account says you can hear the birds but rarely see them, so binoculars help. The flame-breasted fruit dove, coleto, malkoha and ashy thrush also appear in the area's records. Mammals such as the Philippine deer, wild boar, cloud rat and Philippine warty pig, and the water monitor lizard, are said to live here, but visitors are unlikely to meet them in the public zone.
Mount Malabobo is an extinct volcano about
high, and the Baracbac and Basican rivers cross the protected landscape. The average elevation is about
, giving it a forest feel quite different from a lowland spring.
One account reports entrance fees of only a few dozen pesos, so the cost is small. Even entrance and a cottage together are very light compared with a large resort.

items.title: Half-day plan
items.subtitle: Hot springs and a forest walk

children.text: Arrive when it opens. One visitor account lists the hours as
to
, so confirm again before you go.
Pay the entrance fee and rent a cottage. Decide first where to put the food you brought.
Start in the largest, coolest pool and work gradually up to the hot pool near the spring.
Walk the forest paths and climb the view deck for the scenery. Binoculars are useful in the early morning or around sunset when birds are most active.
Eat the food you brought. Some accounts say cooking on site was allowed, but always clean up and take care of your trash yourself.
Enjoy the hot springs once more and head back before late afternoon.
It is best to leave before the forest gets dark. Confirm closing time locally. Since lunch is a packed meal, the pace here is to take your time without other plans.
Enjoy the hot springs and the forest walk at Manleluag.
Head to Balungao Hilltop Adventure and add a zipline ride or a short hike. One travel account that covers both ranks this place just behind Balungao. Check the travel time locally.

items.title: From Manila by car or rental car

children.text: From Manila head north via NLEX and SCTEx. It is about
180km
from Manila, and the address is Barangay Malabobo along Pangasinan-Tarlac Rd.
In your navigation app enter "Manleluag Spring National Park" or "Manleluag Hot Spring". The final stretch is known to be a single-lane concrete road, so take care with larger vehicles.
Check current road conditions and the exact exit in a map app.

Take a bus from Manila toward western Pangasinan (Mangatarem or San Carlos) and transfer to a tricycle in Mangatarem town. No confirmed source gives specific routes or schedules, so check at the terminal.
A visitor account says you can arrive by private vehicle (POV) or tricycle.
The nearest airport is Clark International Airport (CRK). A rental car or chartered vehicle is the easiest option. No confirmed travel time was found.
Paved walkways lead from the entrance to the spring and pool area. The walk is short.
Manleluag sits in a forested area at about
above sea level and may feel slightly cooler than the lowlands, but because the water itself is hot, the relatively cooler dry season is the more comfortable time to go.

The spring water is said to rise from the extinct volcanic terrain of Mount Malabobo and collect in a small cemented reservoir before flowing into the pools. One local description says the groundwater originates in the Zambales Mountains. Because the water is hot, soaking for long is easier in the cool morning and late afternoon than in midday heat, and a rainy day makes the warm water welcome, though you must accept slippery forest paths.
In the rainy season, paths can be slippery and rivers can rise. Monthly temperature data could not be confirmed, so check the local forecast before leaving.

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary with local conditions.

There is little lodging on site. Most people make it a day trip or stay in San Carlos, along the Manila route or near Balungao and travel in. Names and prices change over time, so check the latest information in a map app.

It is fair to assume there are almost no restaurants. A 2018 visitor advised bringing food and drinks because nothing can be bought nearby, and a 2017 account says visitors could cook on site. Rules can change, so ask first about using fire, and be sure to clean up afterward. Packed lunches, fruit, cold water and a thermos of hot water are plenty for a family.
Bring all your food, water and snacks. There are almost no places to buy food nearby.
When entering the springs, do not start at the hottest pool near the spring; begin in the cooler large pool and adjust.
Bring a towel, a change of clothes, sandals, a hat and insect repellent. There is forest, so mosquitoes are possible.
To see birds, walk slowly with binoculars in the early morning. You will hear them more than see them.
If you cook, use the trash bins and leave no litter. This is a protected area.
This is a volcanic area, so some water is very hot. Children must always be accompanied by an adult.
Fees and hours may change, so check the latest notices from the DENR, the local tourism office or the park's Facebook page.
Rather than soaking for a long stretch, move between pools and rest, which is easier on the body. Leave room in your schedule to enjoy the forest and birdsong too.
Fee and facility information relies on 2017–2018 visitor accounts and is dated. Always confirm before visiting.
The water is described as very hot and strongly alkaline at pH 11 to 13. If you have sensitive skin or open wounds, do not soak for long.
The largest pool is about
deep, so children and weak swimmers should take care.
Food and drinking water are hard to find on site, so prepare them in advance.
The last access road is a single lane, so take care when passing oncoming vehicles.
This is a protected area. Do not collect or harm plants or animals, and leave no trash.
